title: 12 First Nations in B.C. buy stake in Coastal GasLink pipeline | CBC News
html:
Politics

12 First Nations in B.C. buy stake in Coastal GasLink pipeline

Piece of ownership secured through $168M federal loan guarantee

A group of 12 First Nations in British Columbia is buying an indirect ownership stake in the Coastal GasLink pipeline, backed by a $168-million loan guarantee from the federal Indigenous Loan Guarantee Program.

On Thursday, CGL First Nations Limited Partnership (CGL FNLP) announced an agreement to purchase an economic interest in an entity owned by TC Energy that holds the company's 35 per cent limited partner stake in the pipeline.

This deal marks the second Indigenous equity partnership to buy into TC Energy's stake in Coastal GasLink this fall, following a $65-million announcement in October for a separate, five-nation coalition.

Together, 17 First Nations along the route now hold an equity interest in the project.

"Our government is building a Canada where Indigenous Peoples are true partners, with the resources and opportunity to pursue their own ambitions and play a leading role in shaping the path forward. That is what meaningful reconciliation looks like in practice," said Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty in a statement.

  • Canada has the opportunity to become a global LNG leader, new report says

  • Coastal GasLink investment deal by TC Energy gives 5 First Nations economic interest

Coastal GasLink is a 670-kilometre pipeline that carries natural gas from near Dawson Creek in northeastern B.C. to the LNG Canada export facility in Kitimat. It is owned by Coastal GasLink Pipeline Limited Partnership, with TC Energy as the operator.

It is the only direct path to the West Coast for natural gas to be liquefied and shipped to Asian markets.

The 12 nations part of the deal include: Cheslatta Carrier Nation, Kitselas First Nation, Lheidli T'enneh First Nation, Nadleh Whut'en First Nation, Nee Tahi Buhn Indian Band, Saik'uz First Nation, Skin Tyee Nation, Stellat'en First Nation, Ts'il Kaz Koh First Nation, Wet'suwet'en First Nation, Witset First Nation and Yekooche First Nation.

The terminal served by the pipeline, LNG Canada, is planning a major Phase 2 expansion, doubling its capacity from 14 to 28 million tonnes a year, putting it on the trajectory to become one of the largest LNG facilities in the world.

The pipeline still faces some First Nations opposition, including from hereditary leaders who had fought its construction through blockades and other protests.

In a statement, Wet'suwet'en and Gitxsan leaders said the existing Coastal GasLink pipeline did not obtain free, prior and informed consent of all impacted nations, nor has the expansion project.

"We respect every nation's right to self-determination, and the reality is this project destroyed our lands without our consent. CGL was built despite Canada and B.C. recognizing in a memorandum that Wet'suwet'en rights and title are held by the Wet'suwet'en Houses under their system of governance," said Wet'suwet'en Hereditary Chief Na'Moks.

The federal Indigenous Loan Guarantee Program provides up to $10 billion in loan guarantees to reduce borrowing costs so Indigenous communities can buy equity stakes in major projects.
summary: A group of 12 First Nations in British Columbia are buying an indirect ownership stake in the Coastal GasLink Pipeline, backed by a $168-million loan guarantee from the federal Indigenous Loan Guarantee Program.
